al-Tirmidhi said after narrating it: It is gharib (strange); we do not know it except through this route, and ʿAmr ibn Abi Khathʿam is weak. al-Bukhari said: he is munkar al-hadith (rejected in narration).

al-Tirmidhi, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Ha-Mim (Ha-Mim), al-Dukhan, on a Friday night, will be forgiven by morning."

al-Tirmidhi said after narrating it: It is gharib; we do not know it except through this route, and Hisham ibn al-Miqdam is considered weak, and al-Hasan did not hear from Abu Hurayrah, as said by Ayyub, Yunus ibn ʿUbayd and ʿAli ibn Zayd. What supports it is what Ibn al-Durays and al-Bayhaqi narrated on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and he mentioned it; and what Ibn al-Durays narrated on the authority of al-Hasan, raised (marfuʿ), with similar wording, but it is mursal (its chain is broken). And what al-Darimi and Muhammad ibn Nasr narrated on the authority of Abu Rafiʿ, who said: "Whoever recites al-Dukhan on Friday night will be forgiven by morning and will be married to the Hur al-ʿIn (wide-eyed maidens)."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated on the authority of Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the surah Ha-Mim, al-Dukhan, on Friday night or on Friday, Allah will build for him a house in Paradise because of it."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Ha-Mim﴾ ﴿By the Clear Book﴾ — the discussion of this, in meaning and grammatical analysis (iʿrab), has already been given in the two surahs preceding this surah.

(p-1349) His saying: ﴿Indeed, We revealed it in a blessed night﴾ is the answer to the oath. If you make the answer "Ha-Mim", then this clause is a new sentence (mustaʾnafah). Some grammarians denied that this clause is the answer to the oath, because it is a description (ṣifah) of the thing sworn by, and the description of the thing sworn by cannot be the answer to the oath. They said the answer is ﴿Indeed, We were ever warning﴾, and Ibn ʿAtiyyah chose this. It was also said that His saying ﴿Indeed, We were ever warning﴾ is a second answer, or a new sentence confirming the revelation, and it has the sense of a cause for it, as if He said: "Indeed, We revealed it because it is part of Our way to warn." The pronoun in "revealed it" refers to the Clear Book, which is the Qur'an.

It was also said: the intended "Book" is all the revealed books, and the pronoun in (revealed it) refers to the Qur'an, meaning that He, glorified is He, swore by all the revealed books that He revealed the Qur'an. The first view is preferable.

The blessed night is the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr), as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We revealed it in the Night of Power﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. It has four names: the Blessed Night, the Night of Acquittal (Layla al-Baraʾah), the Night of the Decree (Layla al-Sakk), and the Night of Power. ʿIkrimah said: the Blessed Night here is the night of the middle of Shaʿban. Qatadah said: the whole Qur'an was sent down in the Night of Power from the Mother of the Book, which is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), to the House of Glory (Bayt al-ʿIzzah) in the lowest heaven. Then Allah, glorified is He, sent it down upon His Prophet (ﷺ) in portions over days and nights during twenty-three years. The detailed discussion of this has already been given in al-Baqarah at His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. Muqatil said: each Night of Power, there would descend from the Tablet of the revelation an amount equal to what Jibril brings down during the year until the same night of the following year. Allah, glorified is He, described this night as blessed because the Qur'an was revealed in it, and it contains the benefits of religion and the world, and because the angels and the Spirit descend in it, as will come in the surah of al-Qadr.

Among its blessings is what Allah, glorified is He, mentioned here by His saying: ﴿In it every wise matter is made distinct﴾. The meaning of "is made distinct" (yufraqu) is: it is separated and clarified, from their saying: "I separated the thing, I separate it, separation." The "wise matter" (amr hakim) is the firmly decreed. That is, Allah, glorified is He, writes in it what will occur during the year: life and death, expansion and contraction, good and evil, and other things. So said Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Hasan and others. This sentence is either another description of the night, with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ), or a new sentence establishing what precedes it.

The majority read yufraqu with a damma on the yaʾ and a fatḥah on the raʾ, lightened. al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash and al-Aʿraj read it with a fatḥah on the yaʾ, a ḍammah on the raʾ, with ﴿every matter﴾ in the accusative and ﴿wise﴾ in the nominative, as the subject.

The truth is what the majority held: that this Blessed Night is the Night of Power, not the middle night of Shaʿban, because Allah, glorified is He, mentioned it generally here and clarified it in al-Baqarah with His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and with His saying in the surah of al-Qadr: ﴿Indeed, We revealed it in the Night of Power﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. After this clear explanation, nothing remains that necessitates disagreement or that requires confusion.

﴿A command from Us﴾. al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: the accusative of "command" (amran) is governed by "is made distinct", meaning "is made distinct as a distinction", because "amran" has the sense of "farqan" (distinction).

The meaning is: We command the explanation of that and its copying (naskh) from the Preserved Tablet. On this view it is accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), like your saying: "he strikes a striking." al-Mubarrad said: "amran" is in the place of a verbal noun, and the estimate is: "We revealed it as a revealing." al-Akhfash said: its accusative is as a circumstantial state (ḥal), meaning "commanding." It was also said it is accusative by specification (ikhtiṣaṣ), meaning: "I mean by this matter a command originating from Us," and in it is an exaltation of the Qur'an's status and magnification of it.

Some scholars mentioned twelve possible readings for the accusative of "amran," the clearest of which is what we have mentioned.

Zayd ibn ʿAli read "amrun" with a nominative: that is, "it is a command." ﴿Indeed, We were ever sending messengers﴾. This sentence is either a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿Indeed, We were ever warning﴾, or a third answer to the oath, or a new sentence.

al-Razi said: the meaning is: We did that warning because We were ever sending messengers to the Prophets.

﴿A mercy from your Lord﴾. The accusative of "mercy" is as a cause: that is, "We revealed it for mercy," said by al-Zajjaj.

al-Mubarrad said: it is accusative as an object of "sending messengers": that is, "We were ever sending messengers, a mercy." It was also said it is a verbal noun in the place of a circumstantial state: that is, "merciful," said by al-Akhfash. al-Hasan read "rahmatun" with a nominative, on the estimate: "it is a mercy."

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, of whoever calls upon Him, the All-Knowing of everything﴾.

Then He, glorified is He, described Himself with what indicates the immensity of His dazzling power, saying: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾. The majority read "Rabbu" with a nominative, in apposition to "the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing", or as the subject of a predicate "There is no god but Him", or as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "He is Lord." The Kufans read "Rabbi" with a genitive, as a substitute for "your Lord", or as an explanation of it, or as a description. ﴿If you are certain﴾ that He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. They had acknowledged this, as Allah related of them in more than one place.

The clause "There is no god but Him" is either a new sentence confirming what precedes it, or the predicate of "Lord of the heavens", as already passed. Likewise the clause ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ is a new sentence confirming what precedes it. ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones﴾. The majority read it with a nominative, as a new sentence with an estimated subject: "He is your Lord," or as a substitute for "Lord of the heavens," or as an explanation or description of it. al-Kisa'i, in the transmission of al-Shirazi from him, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Hayawah and al-Hasan read it with a genitive. The basis for the genitive is what we mentioned in the reading of whoever read "Rabbi" with a genitive in "Lord of the heavens."

﴿Rather, they are in doubt, playing﴾. He turned away from their being certain to their being in doubt concerning monotheism and resurrection, and concerning their acknowledgment that Allah is their Creator and the Creator of all created things, and that this acknowledgment from them is in the manner of play and mockery. The position of "playing" is nominative, as a second predicate, or accusative as a circumstantial state.

﴿So watch for the day when the sky brings a clear smoke﴾. The "fa" (so) marks the sequence of what follows upon what precedes, because their being in doubt and play requires that. The meaning: await for them, O Muhammad, the day when the sky brings a clear smoke. It was also said the meaning is: remember their saying this, so that you may bear witness against them on the day when the sky brings a clear smoke.

It has been disputed concerning this smoke mentioned in the verse: when does it come? It was said: it is among the signs of the Hour, and that it will remain on the earth for forty days. It is established in the Sahih that it is among the ten signs that come before the establishment of the Hour. It was also said: it is a matter that has already passed, namely what befell Quraysh through the Prophet's (ﷺ) supplication, until a man would see between the sky and the earth a smoke. This is established in the two Sahihs and others. That was when the Prophet (ﷺ) invoked against them for years like the years of Yusuf, so famine and hardship befell them until they ate bones, and a man would look at the sky and see between himself and it something like smoke from hardship. It was also said: it is the day of the conquest of Mecca. The evidence for these views will come at the end of the discussion.

His saying: ﴿covering the people﴾ is a second description of "smoke": that is, it encompasses them and surrounds them. ﴿This is a painful punishment﴾: that is, they say "This is a painful punishment," or saying it, or Allah says it to them.

﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed, we are believers﴾: that is, they say this. It is narrated that they came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "If Allah removes this punishment from us, we will embrace Islam." By "the punishment" is meant the hunger which caused what they saw of the smoke, or what they say when they see the smoke which is among the signs of the Hour, or when they saw it on the day of the conquest of Mecca, according to the differing views.

The preponderant view among these is that it is the smoke they imagined from what had come upon them of hardship and severe hunger. Preferring this does not conflict with what has come that smoke is among the signs of the Hour, for that is another smoke. Nor does it conflict with what was said: that it is the one on the day of the conquest of Mecca, for that too is another smoke, on the assumption that its occurrence is sound.

﴿How can they have the reminder?﴾: that is, how can they take heed and be admonished by what has befallen them, when the situation is that a clear Messenger has come to them, who makes clear to them everything they need of the matters of religion and the world.

﴿Then they turned away from him﴾: that is, they turned away from that Messenger who came to them, and did not content themselves with mere aversion from him, but went beyond it. ﴿And they said: "A taught, possessed one"﴾: that is, they said: "He is only taught the Qur'an by a human," and they said "He is possessed," so how would these people be reminded, and how could they have the reminder?

Then, when they called upon Allah to remove the punishment from them, and that if He removed it they would believe, Allah, glorified is He, answered them with His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little﴾: that is, We remove it from them, a slight removal, or for a short time. Then Allah, glorified is He, informed of them that they would not desist from what they were upon of polytheism, and would not fulfil what they had promised of faith. So He said: ﴿Indeed, you will return﴾: that is, to what you were upon of polytheism. This was indeed the case, for when Allah removed that punishment from them, they returned to what they had been upon of disbelief and obstinacy. It was also said the meaning is: "Indeed, you will return to Us by resurrection and rising," and the first is preferable.

﴿The day We seize with the greatest seizing﴾. The adverbial phrase is accusative by an implied "remember". It was also said it is a substitute for ﴿the day the sky brings﴾, and it was said it is connected to "avenging" (muntaqimun), and it was said: to what "avenging" indicates, which is "We will avenge".

The greatest seizing is the Day of Badr, said by most.

The meaning is that when they returned to denial and disbelief after the punishment had been lifted from them, Allah took vengeance on them through the Battle of Badr.

al-Hasan and Ikrimah said that it refers to the punishment of the Fire. al-Zajjaj chose this view, but the first view is preferable.

The majority of reciters (qira'ah) read ﴿نَبْطِشُ﴾ with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the ta', meaning "We will seize with them." al-Hasan and Abu Ja'far read it with a damma on the ta', which is a dialectal form. Abu Raja' and Talhah read it with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the ta'.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿in a blessed night﴾ that he said: The Qur'an was sent down in the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr), and Jibril brought it down upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in installments, in response to the people's questions.

Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿in which every wise matter is made distinct﴾ that he said: In the Night of Power, whatever will happen during the year of provision, death, life and rain is written down from Umm al-Kitab (the Mother of the Book), until it is written that so-and-so will perform the pilgrimage, and so-and-so will perform the pilgrimage.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Umar regarding ﴿in which every wise matter is made distinct﴾ that he said: The matter of one year is (determined) for the next year, except for wretchedness and happiness, for that is in the Book of Allah and is not changed or altered.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who graded it sound (sahih), and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated that he said: You see a man walking in the markets while his name has already been entered among the dead. Then he recited ﴿Indeed, We sent it down in a blessed night﴾ up to the end of the verse, meaning the Night of Power. He said: In that night, the matters of this world are separated for the next year, whether death, life or provision. All the matters of this world are separated in that night for the following year.

Ibn Zanjawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The terms of life are cut off from Sha'ban to Sha'ban, to the extent that a man marries and has children, and his name has already gone out among the dead."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Jarir also narrated it from Uthman ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mughirah ibn al-Akhnas. This is a mursal report (a report whose chain omits a companion), and it cannot serve as evidence, nor can it be set against the clear texts of the Qur'an.

Whatever has been narrated on this subject is either mursal or not sound.

The author of al-Durr al-Manthur (al-Suyuti) included these reports, and he also included what has been narrated about the virtue of the middle night of Sha'ban. However, that does not necessitate that it is what is meant by ﴿a blessed night﴾.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that when Quraysh became stubborn toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and held back from Islam, he said: "O Allah, help me against them with seven years like the seven years of Yusuf." So a famine and hardship struck them until they ate bones. A man would look up at the sky and see between himself and it something like smoke, because of hunger. Then Allah sent down ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾ up to the end of the verse. The Prophet (ﷺ) was approached and it was said: "O Messenger of Allah, ask Allah for rain for Mudar." So he asked for rain for them, and they were given water. Then Allah sent down ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return﴾. When comfort returned to them, they went back to their former state. So Allah sent down ﴿On the Day We will seize with the greatest seizing; indeed, We will take retribution﴾, and Allah took vengeance on them on the Day of Badr. Thus the seizing, the smoke and the enforced punishment (al-lizam) have passed.

Similar reports have been narrated from Ibn Mas'ud through more than one route, and similar ones have been narrated from a group of the Successors (tabi'un).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn Abi Mulaykah that he said: I entered upon Ibn Abbas, and he said: "I did not sleep last night." I asked: "Why?" He said: "The star rose, and I feared that the smoke would come upon us at night."

Ibn Kathir said: This is a sound chain (isnad). al-Suyuti also graded it sound, but it does not state that this was the occasion of revelation of the verse.

We have already explained to you that there is no contradiction between this verse being revealed concerning the smoke that appeared to Quraysh because of hunger, and the smoke being one of the signs and portents of the Hour.

Sound, fair and weak reports have come concerning the latter, but none of them states that it was the occasion of revelation of the verse. There is no need for us to lengthen the discussion by mentioning them. What is obligatory is to hold fast to what is established in the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) and elsewhere: that the smoke of Quraysh at the time of hardship and hunger was the occasion of revelation. By this you will know that the view of those who preferred that it is the smoke that is one of the portents of the Hour, such as Ibn Kathir in his tafsir and others, is refuted. Likewise the view of those who said it is the smoke that occurred on the Day of the Conquest of Mecca, relying on what Ibn Sa'd narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "On the Day of the Conquest of Mecca there was smoke, and this is the saying of Allah: ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾." This does not contradict what is in the two Sahihs, even if its chain is sound, given the possibility that Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) thought that the smoke that occurred on the day of the Conquest was what was meant by the verse. For this reason he did not state explicitly that it was the occasion of its revelation.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah that he said: Ibn Abbas said, and Ibn Mas'ud said: "The greatest seizing is on the Day of Badr," and I say it is the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir said: This is a sound chain.

Ibn Kathir had said before this: Ibn Mas'ud explained it as the Day of Badr. This is the view of a group who agreed with Ibn Mas'ud's explanation of the smoke as what has been mentioned before. It was also narrated from Ibn Abbas through the report of al-Awfi from him, and from Ubayy ibn Ka'b and a group, and it is possible. The apparent meaning is that it is the Day of Resurrection, even though the Day of Badr was also a day of great seizing. End of quotation.

I say: Rather, the apparent meaning is that it is the Day of Badr, even if the Day of Resurrection is a day of a seizing greater than every seizing. The context is about Quraysh, so explaining it as the seizing specific to them is preferable to explaining it as the seizing that will occur on the Day of Resurrection for every sinner among mankind and the jinn.

(p-1351)

al-Razi said: the meaning is: We did that warning because We were ever sending messengers to the Prophets.

﴿A mercy from your Lord﴾. The accusative of "mercy" is as a cause: that is, "We revealed it for mercy," said by al-Zajjaj.

al-Mubarrad said: it is accusative as an object of "sending messengers": that is, "We were ever sending messengers, a mercy." It was also said it is a verbal noun in the place of a circumstantial state: that is, "merciful," said by al-Akhfash. al-Hasan read "rahmatun" with a nominative, on the estimate: "it is a mercy."

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, of whoever calls upon Him, the All-Knowing of everything﴾.

Then He, glorified is He, described Himself with what indicates the immensity of His dazzling power, saying: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾. The majority read "Rabbu" with a nominative, in apposition to "the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing", or as the subject of a predicate "There is no god but Him", or as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "He is Lord." The Kufans read "Rabbi" with a genitive, as a substitute for "your Lord", or as an explanation of it, or as a description. ﴿If you are certain﴾ that He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. They had acknowledged this, as Allah related of them in more than one place.

The clause "There is no god but Him" is either a new sentence confirming what precedes it, or the predicate of "Lord of the heavens", as already passed. Likewise the clause ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ is a new sentence confirming what precedes it. ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones﴾. The majority read it with a nominative, as a new sentence with an estimated subject: "He is your Lord," or as a substitute for "Lord of the heavens," or as an explanation or description of it. al-Kisa'i, in the transmission of al-Shirazi from him, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Hayawah and al-Hasan read it with a genitive. The basis for the genitive is what we mentioned in the reading of whoever read "Rabbi" with a genitive in "Lord of the heavens."

﴿Rather, they are in doubt, playing﴾. He turned away from their being certain to their being in doubt concerning monotheism and resurrection, and concerning their acknowledgment that Allah is their Creator and the Creator of all created things, and that this acknowledgment from them is in the manner of play and mockery. The position of "playing" is nominative, as a second predicate, or accusative as a circumstantial state.

﴿So watch for the day when the sky brings a clear smoke﴾. The "fa" (so) marks the sequence of what follows upon what precedes, because their being in doubt and play requires that. The meaning: await for them, O Muhammad, the day when the sky brings a clear smoke. It was also said the meaning is: remember their saying this, so that you may bear witness against them on the day when the sky brings a clear smoke.

It has been disputed concerning this smoke mentioned in the verse: when does it come? It was said: it is among the signs of the Hour, and that it will remain on the earth for forty days. It is established in the Sahih that it is among the ten signs that come before the establishment of the Hour. It was also said: it is a matter that has already passed, namely what befell Quraysh through the Prophet's (ﷺ) supplication, until a man would see between the sky and the earth a smoke. This is established in the two Sahihs and others. That was when the Prophet (ﷺ) invoked against them for years like the years of Yusuf, so famine and hardship befell them until they ate bones, and a man would look at the sky and see between himself and it something like smoke from hardship. It was also said: it is the day of the conquest of Mecca. The evidence for these views will come at the end of the discussion.

His saying: ﴿covering the people﴾ is a second description of "smoke": that is, it encompasses them and surrounds them. ﴿This is a painful punishment﴾: that is, they say "This is a painful punishment," or saying it, or Allah says it to them.

﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed, we are believers﴾: that is, they say this. It is narrated that they came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "If Allah removes this punishment from us, we will embrace Islam." By "the punishment" is meant the hunger which caused what they saw of the smoke, or what they say when they see the smoke which is among the signs of the Hour, or when they saw it on the day of the conquest of Mecca, according to the differing views.

The preponderant view among these is that it is the smoke they imagined from what had come upon them of hardship and severe hunger. Preferring this does not conflict with what has come that smoke is among the signs of the Hour, for that is another smoke. Nor does it conflict with what was said: that it is the one on the day of the conquest of Mecca, for that too is another smoke, on the assumption that its occurrence is sound.

﴿How can they have the reminder?﴾: that is, how can they take heed and be admonished by what has befallen them, when the situation is that a clear Messenger has come to them, who makes clear to them everything they need of the matters of religion and the world.

﴿Then they turned away from him﴾: that is, they turned away from that Messenger who came to them, and did not content themselves with mere aversion from him, but went beyond it. ﴿And they said: "A taught, possessed one"﴾: that is, they said: "He is only taught the Qur'an by a human," and they said "He is possessed," so how would these people be reminded, and how could they have the reminder?

Then, when they called upon Allah to remove the punishment from them, and that if He removed it they would believe, Allah, glorified is He, answered them with His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little﴾: that is, We remove it from them, a slight removal, or for a short time. Then Allah, glorified is He, informed of them that they would not desist from what they were upon of polytheism, and would not fulfil what they had promised of faith. So He said: ﴿Indeed, you will return﴾: that is, to what you were upon of polytheism. This was indeed the case, for when Allah removed that punishment from them, they returned to what they had been upon of disbelief and obstinacy. It was also said the meaning is: "Indeed, you will return to Us by resurrection and rising," and the first is preferable.

﴿The day We seize with the greatest seizing﴾. The adverbial phrase is accusative by an implied "remember". It was also said it is a substitute for ﴿the day the sky brings﴾, and it was said it is connected to "avenging" (muntaqimun), and it was said: to what "avenging" indicates, which is "We will avenge".

The greatest seizing is the Day of Badr, said by most.

The meaning is that when they returned to denial and disbelief after the punishment had been lifted from them, Allah took vengeance on them through the Battle of Badr.

al-Hasan and Ikrimah said that it refers to the punishment of the Fire. al-Zajjaj chose this view, but the first view is preferable.

The majority of reciters (qira'ah) read ﴿نَبْطِشُ﴾ with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the ta', meaning "We will seize with them." al-Hasan and Abu Ja'far read it with a damma on the ta', which is a dialectal form. Abu Raja' and Talhah read it with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the ta'.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿in a blessed night﴾ that he said: The Qur'an was sent down in the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr), and Jibril brought it down upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in installments, in response to the people's questions.

Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿in which every wise matter is made distinct﴾ that he said: In the Night of Power, whatever will happen during the year of provision, death, life and rain is written down from Umm al-Kitab (the Mother of the Book), until it is written that so-and-so will perform the pilgrimage, and so-and-so will perform the pilgrimage.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Umar regarding ﴿in which every wise matter is made distinct﴾ that he said: The matter of one year is (determined) for the next year, except for wretchedness and happiness, for that is in the Book of Allah and is not changed or altered.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who graded it sound (sahih), and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated that he said: You see a man walking in the markets while his name has already been entered among the dead. Then he recited ﴿Indeed, We sent it down in a blessed night﴾ up to the end of the verse, meaning the Night of Power. He said: In that night, the matters of this world are separated for the next year, whether death, life or provision. All the matters of this world are separated in that night for the following year.

Ibn Zanjawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The terms of life are cut off from Sha'ban to Sha'ban, to the extent that a man marries and has children, and his name has already gone out among the dead."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Jarir also narrated it from Uthman ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mughirah ibn al-Akhnas. This is a mursal report (a report whose chain omits a companion), and it cannot serve as evidence, nor can it be set against the clear texts of the Qur'an.

Whatever has been narrated on this subject is either mursal or not sound.

The author of al-Durr al-Manthur (al-Suyuti) included these reports, and he also included what has been narrated about the virtue of the middle night of Sha'ban. However, that does not necessitate that it is what is meant by ﴿a blessed night﴾.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that when Quraysh became stubborn toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and held back from Islam, he said: "O Allah, help me against them with seven years like the seven years of Yusuf." So a famine and hardship struck them until they ate bones. A man would look up at the sky and see between himself and it something like smoke, because of hunger. Then Allah sent down ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾ up to the end of the verse. The Prophet (ﷺ) was approached and it was said: "O Messenger of Allah, ask Allah for rain for Mudar." So he asked for rain for them, and they were given water. Then Allah sent down ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return﴾. When comfort returned to them, they went back to their former state. So Allah sent down ﴿On the Day We will seize with the greatest seizing; indeed, We will take retribution﴾, and Allah took vengeance on them on the Day of Badr. Thus the seizing, the smoke and the enforced punishment (al-lizam) have passed.

Similar reports have been narrated from Ibn Mas'ud through more than one route, and similar ones have been narrated from a group of the Successors (tabi'un).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn Abi Mulaykah that he said: I entered upon Ibn Abbas, and he said: "I did not sleep last night." I asked: "Why?" He said: "The star rose, and I feared that the smoke would come upon us at night."

Ibn Kathir said: This is a sound chain (isnad). al-Suyuti also graded it sound, but it does not state that this was the occasion of revelation of the verse.

We have already explained to you that there is no contradiction between this verse being revealed concerning the smoke that appeared to Quraysh because of hunger, and the smoke being one of the signs and portents of the Hour.

Sound, fair and weak reports have come concerning the latter, but none of them states that it was the occasion of revelation of the verse. There is no need for us to lengthen the discussion by mentioning them. What is obligatory is to hold fast to what is established in the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) and elsewhere: that the smoke of Quraysh at the time of hardship and hunger was the occasion of revelation. By this you will know that the view of those who preferred that it is the smoke that is one of the portents of the Hour, such as Ibn Kathir in his tafsir and others, is refuted. Likewise the view of those who said it is the smoke that occurred on the Day of the Conquest of Mecca, relying on what Ibn Sa'd narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "On the Day of the Conquest of Mecca there was smoke, and this is the saying of Allah: ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾." This does not contradict what is in the two Sahihs, even if its chain is sound, given the possibility that Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) thought that the smoke that occurred on the day of the Conquest was what was meant by the verse. For this reason he did not state explicitly that it was the occasion of its revelation.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah that he said: Ibn Abbas said, and Ibn Mas'ud said: "The greatest seizing is on the Day of Badr," and I say it is the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir said: This is a sound chain.

Ibn Kathir had said before this: Ibn Mas'ud explained it as the Day of Badr. This is the view of a group who agreed with Ibn Mas'ud's explanation of the smoke as what has been mentioned before. It was also narrated from Ibn Abbas through the report of al-Awfi from him, and from Ubayy ibn Ka'b and a group, and it is possible. The apparent meaning is that it is the Day of Resurrection, even though the Day of Badr was also a day of great seizing. End of quotation.

I say: Rather, the apparent meaning is that it is the Day of Badr, even if the Day of Resurrection is a day of a seizing greater than every seizing. The context is about Quraysh, so explaining it as the seizing specific to them is preferable to explaining it as the seizing that will occur on the Day of Resurrection for every sinner among mankind and the jinn.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 44, verse 1–33 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Qurtubi said: It is Meccan by consensus, except His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15].

Ibn Mardawayh narrated, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, that Surat al-Dukhan was revealed in Mecca.

al-Tirmidhi and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab narrated, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Ha-Mim, al-Dukhan, in a night, seventy thousand angels will seek forgiveness for him by morning."

al-Tirmidhi said after narrating it: It is gharib (strange); we do not know it except through this route, and ʿAmr ibn Abi Khathʿam is weak. al-Bukhari said: he is munkar al-hadith (rejected in narration).

al-Tirmidhi, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Ha-Mim (Ha-Mim), al-Dukhan, on a Friday night, will be forgiven by morning."

al-Tirmidhi said after narrating it: It is gharib; we do not know it except through this route, and Hisham ibn al-Miqdam is considered weak, and al-Hasan did not hear from Abu Hurayrah, as said by Ayyub, Yunus ibn ʿUbayd and ʿAli ibn Zayd. What supports it is what Ibn al-Durays and al-Bayhaqi narrated on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and he mentioned it; and what Ibn al-Durays narrated on the authority of al-Hasan, raised (marfuʿ), with similar wording, but it is mursal (its chain is broken). And what al-Darimi and Muhammad ibn Nasr narrated on the authority of Abu Rafiʿ, who said: "Whoever recites al-Dukhan on Friday night will be forgiven by morning and will be married to the Hur al-ʿIn (wide-eyed maidens)."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated on the authority of Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the surah Ha-Mim, al-Dukhan, on Friday night or on Friday, Allah will build for him a house in Paradise because of it."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Ha-Mim﴾ ﴿By the Clear Book﴾ — the discussion of this, in meaning and grammatical analysis (iʿrab), has already been given in the two surahs preceding this surah.

Some grammarians denied that this clause is the answer to the oath, because it is a description (ṣifah) of the thing sworn by, and the description of the thing sworn by cannot be the answer to the oath. They said the answer is ﴿Indeed, We were ever warning﴾, and Ibn ʿAtiyyah chose this. It was also said that His saying ﴿Indeed, We were ever warning﴾ is a second answer, or a new sentence confirming the revelation, and it has the sense of a cause for it, as if He said: "Indeed, We revealed it because it is part of Our way to warn." The pronoun in "revealed it" refers to the Clear Book, which is the Qur'an.

It was also said: the intended "Book" is all the revealed books, and the pronoun in (revealed it) refers to the Qur'an, meaning that He, glorified is He, swore by all the revealed books that He revealed the Qur'an. The first view is preferable.

The blessed night is the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr), as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We revealed it in the Night of Power﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. It has four names: the Blessed Night, the Night of Acquittal (Layla al-Baraʾah), the Night of the Decree (Layla al-Sakk), and the Night of Power. ʿIkrimah said: the Blessed Night here is the night of the middle of Shaʿban. Qatadah said: the whole Qur'an was sent down in the Night of Power from the Mother of the Book, which is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), to the House of Glory (Bayt al-ʿIzzah) in the lowest heaven. Then Allah, glorified is He, sent it down upon His Prophet (ﷺ) in portions over days and nights during twenty-three years. The detailed discussion of this has already been given in al-Baqarah at His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. Muqatil said: each Night of Power, there would descend from the Tablet of the revelation an amount equal to what Jibril brings down during the year until the same night of the following year. Allah, glorified is He, described this night as blessed because the Qur'an was revealed in it, and it contains the benefits of religion and the world, and because the angels and the Spirit descend in it, as will come in the surah of al-Qadr.

Among its blessings is what Allah, glorified is He, mentioned here by His saying: ﴿In it every wise matter is made distinct﴾. The meaning of "is made distinct" (yufraqu) is: it is separated and clarified, from their saying: "I separated the thing, I separate it, separation." The "wise matter" (amr hakim) is the firmly decreed. That is, Allah, glorified is He, writes in it what will occur during the year: life and death, expansion and contraction, good and evil, and other things. So said Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Hasan and others. This sentence is either another description of the night, with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ), or a new sentence establishing what precedes it.

The majority read yufraqu with a damma on the yaʾ and a fatḥah on the raʾ, lightened. al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash and al-Aʿraj read it with a fatḥah on the yaʾ, a ḍammah on the raʾ, with ﴿every matter﴾ in the accusative and ﴿wise﴾ in the nominative, as the subject.

The truth is what the majority held: that this Blessed Night is the Night of Power, not the middle night of Shaʿban, because Allah, glorified is He, mentioned it generally here and clarified it in al-Baqarah with His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and with His saying in the surah of al-Qadr: ﴿Indeed, We revealed it in the Night of Power﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿in a blessed night﴾ that he said: The Qur'an was sent down in the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr), and Jibril brought it down upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in installments, in response to the people's questions.

Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿in which every wise matter is made distinct﴾ that he said: In the Night of Power, whatever will happen during the year of provision, death, life and rain is written down from Umm al-Kitab (the Mother of the Book), until it is written that so-and-so will perform the pilgrimage, and so-and-so will perform the pilgrimage.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Umar regarding ﴿in which every wise matter is made distinct﴾ that he said: The matter of one year is (determined) for the next year, except for wretchedness and happiness, for that is in the Book of Allah and is not changed or altered.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who graded it sound (sahih), and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated that he said: You see a man walking in the markets while his name has already been entered among the dead. Then he recited ﴿Indeed, We sent it down in a blessed night﴾ up to the end of the verse, meaning the Night of Power. He said: In that night, the matters of this world are separated for the next year, whether death, life or provision. All the matters of this world are separated in that night for the following year.

Ibn Zanjawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The terms of life are cut off from Sha'ban to Sha'ban, to the extent that a man marries and has children, and his name has already gone out among the dead."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Jarir also narrated it from Uthman ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mughirah ibn al-Akhnas. This is a mursal report (a report whose chain omits a companion), and it cannot serve as evidence, nor can it be set against the clear texts of the Qur'an.

Whatever has been narrated on this subject is either mursal or not sound.

The author of al-Durr al-Manthur (al-Suyuti) included these reports, and he also included what has been narrated about the virtue of the middle night of Sha'ban. However, that does not necessitate that it is what is meant by ﴿a blessed night﴾.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that when Quraysh became stubborn toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and held back from Islam, he said: "O Allah, help me against them with seven years like the seven years of Yusuf." So a famine and hardship struck them until they ate bones. A man would look up at the sky and see between himself and it something like smoke, because of hunger. Then Allah sent down ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾ up to the end of the verse. The Prophet (ﷺ) was approached and it was said: "O Messenger of Allah, ask Allah for rain for Mudar." So he asked for rain for them, and they were given water. Then Allah sent down ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed, you will return﴾. When comfort returned to them, they went back to their former state. So Allah sent down ﴿On the Day We will seize with the greatest seizing; indeed, We will take retribution﴾, and Allah took vengeance on them on the Day of Badr. Thus the seizing, the smoke and the enforced punishment (al-lizam) have passed.

Similar reports have been narrated from Ibn Mas'ud through more than one route, and similar ones have been narrated from a group of the Successors (tabi'un).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn Abi Mulaykah that he said: I entered upon Ibn Abbas, and he said: "I did not sleep last night." I asked: "Why?" He said: "The star rose, and I feared that the smoke would come upon us at night."

Ibn Kathir said: This is a sound chain (isnad). al-Suyuti also graded it sound, but it does not state that this was the occasion of revelation of the verse.

We have already explained to you that there is no contradiction between this verse being revealed concerning the smoke that appeared to Quraysh because of hunger, and the smoke being one of the signs and portents of the Hour.

Sound, fair and weak reports have come concerning the latter, but none of them states that it was the occasion of revelation of the verse. There is no need for us to lengthen the discussion by mentioning them. What is obligatory is to hold fast to what is established in the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) and elsewhere: that the smoke of Quraysh at the time of hardship and hunger was the occasion of revelation. By this you will know that the view of those who preferred that it is the smoke that is one of the portents of the Hour, such as Ibn Kathir in his tafsir and others, is refuted. Likewise the view of those who said it is the smoke that occurred on the Day of the Conquest of Mecca, relying on what Ibn Sa'd narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "On the Day of the Conquest of Mecca there was smoke, and this is the saying of Allah: ﴿So watch for the Day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾." This does not contradict what is in the two Sahihs, even if its chain is sound, given the possibility that Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) thought that the smoke that occurred on the day of the Conquest was what was meant by the verse. For this reason he did not state explicitly that it was the occasion of its revelation.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah that he said: Ibn Abbas said, and Ibn Mas'ud said: "The greatest seizing is on the Day of Badr," and I say it is the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir said: This is a sound chain.

Ibn Kathir had said before this: Ibn Mas'ud explained it as the Day of Badr. This is the view of a group who agreed with Ibn Mas'ud's explanation of the smoke as what has been mentioned before. It was also narrated from Ibn Abbas through the report of al-Awfi from him, and from Ubayy ibn Ka'b and a group, and it is possible. The apparent meaning is that it is the Day of Resurrection, even though the Day of Badr was also a day of great seizing. End of quotation.

I say: Rather, the apparent meaning is that it is the Day of Badr, even if the Day of Resurrection is a day of a seizing greater than every seizing. The context is about Quraysh, so explaining it as the seizing specific to them is preferable to explaining it as the seizing that will occur on the Day of Resurrection for every sinner among mankind and the jinn.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 44, verse 1–33 (part 1 of 2):

Al-Qurtubi said: It is Meccan by consensus, except His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15].

Ibn Mardawayh narrated, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, that Surat al-Dukhan was revealed in Mecca.

al-Tirmidhi and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab narrated, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Ha-Mim, al-Dukhan, in a night, seventy thousand angels will seek forgiveness for him by morning."

al-Tirmidhi said after narrating it: It is gharib (strange); we do not know it except through this route, and ʿAmr ibn Abi Khathʿam is weak. al-Bukhari said: he is munkar al-hadith (rejected in narration).

al-Tirmidhi, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Ha-Mim (Ha-Mim), al-Dukhan, on a Friday night, will be forgiven by morning."

al-Tirmidhi said after narrating it: It is gharib; we do not know it except through this route, and Hisham ibn al-Miqdam is considered weak, and al-Hasan did not hear from Abu Hurayrah, as said by Ayyub, Yunus ibn ʿUbayd and ʿAli ibn Zayd. What supports it is what Ibn al-Durays and al-Bayhaqi narrated on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and he mentioned it; and what Ibn al-Durays narrated on the authority of al-Hasan, raised (marfuʿ), with similar wording, but it is mursal (its chain is broken). And what al-Darimi and Muhammad ibn Nasr narrated on the authority of Abu Rafiʿ, who said: "Whoever recites al-Dukhan on Friday night will be forgiven by morning and will be married to the Hur al-ʿIn (wide-eyed maidens)."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated on the authority of Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the surah Ha-Mim, al-Dukhan, on Friday night or on Friday, Allah will build for him a house in Paradise because of it."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Ha-Mim﴾ ﴿By the Clear Book﴾ — the discussion of this, in meaning and grammatical analysis (iʿrab), has already been given in the two surahs preceding this surah.

(p-1349) His saying: ﴿Indeed, We revealed it in a blessed night﴾ is the answer to the oath. If you make the answer "Ha-Mim", then this clause is a new sentence (mustaʾnafah). Some grammarians denied that this clause is the answer to the oath, because it is a description (ṣifah) of the thing sworn by, and the description of the thing sworn by cannot be the answer to the oath. They said the answer is ﴿Indeed, We were ever warning﴾, and Ibn ʿAtiyyah chose this. It was also said that His saying ﴿Indeed, We were ever warning﴾ is a second answer, or a new sentence confirming the revelation, and it has the sense of a cause for it, as if He said: "Indeed, We revealed it because it is part of Our way to warn." The pronoun in "revealed it" refers to the Clear Book, which is the Qur'an.

It was also said: the intended "Book" is all the revealed books, and the pronoun in (revealed it) refers to the Qur'an, meaning that He, glorified is He, swore by all the revealed books that He revealed the Qur'an. The first view is preferable.

The blessed night is the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr), as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We revealed it in the Night of Power﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. It has four names: the Blessed Night, the Night of Acquittal (Layla al-Baraʾah), the Night of the Decree (Layla al-Sakk), and the Night of Power. ʿIkrimah said: the Blessed Night here is the night of the middle of Shaʿban. Qatadah said: the whole Qur'an was sent down in the Night of Power from the Mother of the Book, which is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), to the House of Glory (Bayt al-ʿIzzah) in the lowest heaven. Then Allah, glorified is He, sent it down upon His Prophet (ﷺ) in portions over days and nights during twenty-three years. The detailed discussion of this has already been given in al-Baqarah at His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. Muqatil said: each Night of Power, there would descend from the Tablet of the revelation an amount equal to what Jibril brings down during the year until the same night of the following year. Allah, glorified is He, described this night as blessed because the Qur'an was revealed in it, and it contains the benefits of religion and the world, and because the angels and the Spirit descend in it, as will come in the surah of al-Qadr.

Among its blessings is what Allah, glorified is He, mentioned here by His saying: ﴿In it every wise matter is made distinct﴾. The meaning of "is made distinct" (yufraqu) is: it is separated and clarified, from their saying: "I separated the thing, I separate it, separation." The "wise matter" (amr hakim) is the firmly decreed. That is, Allah, glorified is He, writes in it what will occur during the year: life and death, expansion and contraction, good and evil, and other things. So said Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Hasan and others. This sentence is either another description of the night, with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ), or a new sentence establishing what precedes it.

The majority read yufraqu with a damma on the yaʾ and a fatḥah on the raʾ, lightened. al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash and al-Aʿraj read it with a fatḥah on the yaʾ, a ḍammah on the raʾ, with ﴿every matter﴾ in the accusative and ﴿wise﴾ in the nominative, as the subject.

The truth is what the majority held: that this Blessed Night is the Night of Power, not the middle night of Shaʿban, because Allah, glorified is He, mentioned it generally here and clarified it in al-Baqarah with His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], and with His saying in the surah of al-Qadr: ﴿Indeed, We revealed it in the Night of Power﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. After this clear explanation, nothing remains that necessitates disagreement or that requires confusion.

﴿A command from Us﴾. al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: the accusative of "command" (amran) is governed by "is made distinct", meaning "is made distinct as a distinction", because "amran" has the sense of "farqan" (distinction).

The meaning is: We command the explanation of that and its copying (naskh) from the Preserved Tablet. On this view it is accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), like your saying: "he strikes a striking." al-Mubarrad said: "amran" is in the place of a verbal noun, and the estimate is: "We revealed it as a revealing." al-Akhfash said: its accusative is as a circumstantial state (ḥal), meaning "commanding." It was also said it is accusative by specification (ikhtiṣaṣ), meaning: "I mean by this matter a command originating from Us," and in it is an exaltation of the Qur'an's status and magnification of it.

Some scholars mentioned twelve possible readings for the accusative of "amran," the clearest of which is what we have mentioned.

Zayd ibn ʿAli read "amrun" with a nominative: that is, "it is a command." ﴿Indeed, We were ever sending messengers﴾. This sentence is either a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿Indeed, We were ever warning﴾, or a third answer to the oath, or a new sentence.

al-Razi said: the meaning is: We did that warning because We were ever sending messengers to the Prophets.

﴿A mercy from your Lord﴾. The accusative of "mercy" is as a cause: that is, "We revealed it for mercy," said by al-Zajjaj.

al-Mubarrad said: it is accusative as an object of "sending messengers": that is, "We were ever sending messengers, a mercy." It was also said it is a verbal noun in the place of a circumstantial state: that is, "merciful," said by al-Akhfash. al-Hasan read "rahmatun" with a nominative, on the estimate: "it is a mercy."

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, of whoever calls upon Him, the All-Knowing of everything﴾.

Then He, glorified is He, described Himself with what indicates the immensity of His dazzling power, saying: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾. The majority read "Rabbu" with a nominative, in apposition to "the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing", or as the subject of a predicate "There is no god but Him", or as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "He is Lord." The Kufans read "Rabbi" with a genitive, as a substitute for "your Lord", or as an explanation of it, or as a description. ﴿If you are certain﴾ that He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. They had acknowledged this, as Allah related of them in more than one place.

The clause "There is no god but Him" is either a new sentence confirming what precedes it, or the predicate of "Lord of the heavens", as already passed. Likewise the clause ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ is a new sentence confirming what precedes it. ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones﴾. The majority read it with a nominative, as a new sentence with an estimated subject: "He is your Lord," or as a substitute for "Lord of the heavens," or as an explanation or description of it. al-Kisa'i, in the transmission of al-Shirazi from him, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Hayawah and al-Hasan read it with a genitive. The basis for the genitive is what we mentioned in the reading of whoever read "Rabbi" with a genitive in "Lord of the heavens."

﴿Rather, they are in doubt, playing﴾. He turned away from their being certain to their being in doubt concerning monotheism and resurrection, and concerning their acknowledgment that Allah is their Creator and the Creator of all created things, and that this acknowledgment from them is in the manner of play and mockery. The position of "playing" is nominative, as a second predicate, or accusative as a circumstantial state.

The meaning: await for them, O Muhammad, the day when the sky brings a clear smoke. It was also said the meaning is: remember their saying this, so that you may bear witness against them on the day when the sky brings a clear smoke.

It has been disputed concerning this smoke mentioned in the verse: when does it come? It was said: it is among the signs of the Hour, and that it will remain on the earth for forty days. It is established in the Sahih that it is among the ten signs that come before the establishment of the Hour. It was also said: it is a matter that has already passed, namely what befell Quraysh through the Prophet's (ﷺ) supplication, until a man would see between the sky and the earth a smoke. It is narrated that they came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "If Allah removes this punishment from us, we will embrace Islam." By "the punishment" is meant the hunger which caused what they saw of the smoke, or what they say when they see the smoke which is among the signs of the Hour, or when they saw it on the day of the conquest of Mecca, according to the differing views.

The preponderant view among these is that it is the smoke they imagined from what had come upon them of hardship and severe hunger. Preferring this does not conflict with what has come that smoke is among the signs of the Hour, for that is another smoke. Nor does it conflict with what was said: that it is the one on the day of the conquest of Mecca, for that too is another smoke, on the assumption that its occurrence is sound.

﴿How can they have the reminder?﴾: that is, how can they take heed and be admonished by what has befallen them, when the situation is that a clear Messenger has come to them, who makes clear to them everything they need of the matters of religion and the world.

﴿Then they turned away from him﴾: that is, they turned away from that Messenger who came to them, and did not content themselves with mere aversion from him, but went beyond it. ﴿And they said: "A taught, possessed one"﴾: that is, they said: "He is only taught the Qur'an by a human," and they said "He is possessed," so how would these people be reminded, and how could they have the reminder?

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed of them that they would not desist from what they were upon of polytheism, and would not fulfil what they had promised of faith. So He said: ﴿Indeed, you will return﴾: that is, to what you were upon of polytheism. This was indeed the case, for when Allah removed that punishment from them, they returned to what they had been upon of disbelief and obstinacy. It was also said the meaning is: "Indeed, you will return to Us by resurrection and rising," and the first is preferable.

﴿The day We seize with the greatest seizing﴾. The adverbial phrase is accusative by an implied "remember". It was also said it is a substitute for ﴿the day the sky brings﴾, and it was said it is connected to "avenging" (muntaqimun), and it was said: to what "avenging" indicates, which is "We will avenge".

The greatest seizing is the Day of Badr, said by most.

The meaning is that when they returned to denial and disbelief after the punishment had been lifted from them, Allah took vengeance on them through the Battle of Badr.
