Then, when they did not affirm him and did not answer his call, he returned to his Lord with supplication, as Allah related of him in His saying: ﴿So he called upon his Lord, that these are a criminal people.﴾ The majority read the hamza with a fatha, by supposing a dropped preposition, i.e., "he called upon Him with [the statement] that these are..." Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Isa ibn Umar read it with a kasra, by supposing "saying." In the speech there is an ellipsis, i.e., "so they disbelieved, so he called upon his Lord." The "mujrimun" are the disbelievers. He called it supplication even though he mentioned only the fact of their being criminals, because they had by that deserved his supplication against them.

﴿So travel by night with My servants﴾. Allah, glorified is He, answered his supplication, and commanded that he travel by night with the Children of Israel. It is said "sara" and "asra," both being dialectal forms. The majority read "fa-asri" with a cut (hamzat al-qat'), and the people of the Hijaz read it with a wasl (linking), and Ibn Kathir agreed with them. So the first reading is from "asra," and the second from "sara." The clause is by supposing "saying," i.e., Allah said to Musa: "Travel by night with My servants." ﴿Indeed you will be pursued﴾, meaning: Pharaoh and his hosts will follow you, and the departure of Pharaoh after them has been mentioned in more than one place.

﴿And leave the sea parted﴾, meaning: still, as is said: "raha yarhu rahwan" when it becomes still and does not move.

Al-Jawhari said: it is said "af'al dhalika rahwan," meaning: calmly, in your state; and "ʿaysh rāh," meaning: still. "Raha al-bahr" means the sea became still. Al-Harawi and others said likewise, and this is the known meaning in the language. From it is the poet's saying:

*And the horses prance rahwan in their bridles, like birds escaping from the shurnub with its fur.*

That is: the horses prance in their bridles while still. The meaning is: leave the sea still in its state after you have struck it with your staff, and do not command it to return, as it was, so that the family of Pharaoh enter it after you and after the Children of Israel, (p-1352) and it close over them, and they drown.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "raha bayna rijlayhi rahwan," meaning: he opened them wide. He said: from it is His saying: ﴿And leave the sea parted﴾, meaning: leave it open, as it was after your entering into it. Abu 'Ubayd said likewise, and Mujahid and others said so. Ibn 'Arafa said: both return to one meaning, even if their wording differs, because when the sea's flow is still, it opens. Al-Harawi said: it is possible that "rahwan" is an adjective for Musa, i.e., "travel calmly in your state." Ka'b and al-Hasan said "rahwan" means "a path." Al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' said: "easy."

ʿIkrima said: "dry," as in His saying: ﴿So strike for them a dry path in the sea﴾ [Ta-Ha: 77]. On every reckoning, the meaning is: leave it in a state of rahw, or leave it "rahwan," for emphasis in describing by the verbal noun. ﴿Indeed they are a drowned host﴾, meaning: indeed Pharaoh and his people are drowned.

Allah, glorified is He, informed Musa of this so that his heart would be at rest and his resolve would be steadied.

The majority read "inna" with a kasra as a fresh sentence, for the purpose of informing of this; it is also read with a fatha, by supposing "li-annahum."

﴿How many they left behind of gardens and springs﴾: "kam" here is the informative "kam," which indicates multiplicity. The discussion of the meaning of this verse has passed in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

The majority read "wa-maqamin" with a fatha on the mim, as a noun of place for standing. Ibn Hurmuz, Qatadah, al-Sumayfa', and it is reported from Nafi' with a damma, meaning a place of dwelling.

﴿And luxury in which they were fruit-eaters/merry﴾. "Nima" with a fatha means luxury (al-tanaʿʿum): it is said "naʿʿamahu Allah" and "nāʿamahu," so he became luxurious. With a kasra it means favour (al-minnah) and what Allah bestowed upon you; "fulan wasi' al-ni'mah" means he is wealthy. Al-Jawhari mentioned this meaning.

The majority read "fakihin" with an alif. Abu Raja', al-Hasan, Abu al-Ashhab, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, and Shayba read "fakihin" without an alif. The meaning in the first reading is: enjoying luxury, their souls content; in the second: insolent and wanton.

Al-Jawhari said: "fakiha al-rajul" with a kasra means he is "fakih" when he is good-natured and joking; "al-fakih" also means insolent and wanton. He said: "wa-fakihin" means luxurious. Al-Tha'labi said: both are dialects, like "hadhir" and "hadhar," and "farih" and "farih." It was said: "al-fakih" is one who enjoys all kinds of pleasure, as a man enjoys all kinds of fruit.

﴿Thus, and We made them inherit another people﴾. The "ka" is in the nominative position, as a predicate of an omitted subject. Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., "the matter is thus." It may also be in the accusative position, with the reference being to the verbal noun of a verb indicated by "they left," i.e., "like that deprivation We deprived them of it." It was also said: "like that expulsion We expelled them from it," and it was said: "like that destruction We destroyed them."

On the first reading, "wa-awrathnaha" is coordinated with "taraku"; on the latter readings, it is coordinated with the supposed verb.

By "another people" is meant the Children of Israel, for Allah made them possess the land of Egypt after they had been enslaved in it, so they became its inheritors, i.e., it came to them as inheritance comes to an heir. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿And We made the people who were oppressed inherit the eastern and western parts of the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 137].

﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep over them﴾. This is a statement of their being unconcerned by their destruction.

The exegetes said: that is, they had not been doing righteous deeds on earth for which the earth would weep over them, and no good deed of theirs ascended to heaven for which it would be wept over. The meaning is that no one among the people of heaven or the people of earth was afflicted by their loss and destruction. The Arabs used to say, upon the death of a chief among them: "the heaven and the earth wept for him," meaning his calamity was widespread. From this is Jarir's saying:

*When the news of al-Zubayr came, the walls of Madina humbled themselves, and the lofty mountains.*

From it is also al-Nabigha's saying:

*Harith al-Jawlan wept for the loss of his lord, and Hawran, humbled and shrunken, wept with him.*

Al-Hasan said: there is an omitted annexed noun in the speech, i.e., "the people of heaven and earth, of angels and men, did not weep over them."

Mujahid said: indeed the heaven and the earth weep over the believer for forty mornings. It was said: he is wept for by the places of his prayer and the ascending paths of his deeds. ﴿And they were not given respite﴾, meaning: not granted a delay to another time; rather they were hastened into punishment because of the extremity of their disbelief and the severity of their obstinacy.

﴿And indeed We delivered the Children of Israel from the humiliating punishment﴾, meaning: We rescued them, by destroying their enemy, from what they were in of enslavement, the killing of sons, the sparing of women, and the imposition of hard labour upon them.

His saying "from Pharaoh" is an apposition to "the punishment," either by an omitted annexed noun, i.e., "from the punishment of Pharaoh," or for emphasis, as if he were the punishment itself, so it is substituted for it; or it is a circumstantial clause of "the punishment," the sense being "issuing from Pharaoh." Ibn 'Abbas read "man Fir'awn" with a fatha on the mim, as an interrogative of contempt, as one says to someone who boasts of his lineage or ancestry: "Who are you?"

Then He, glorified is He, explained his condition, saying: ﴿Indeed he was haughty among the extravagant﴾, meaning: haughty in arrogance and tyranny, among the extravagant in disbelief in Allah and in committing His sins, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4].

When He, glorified is He, explained the manner in which He removed harm from the Children of Israel, He explained what He honoured them with, saying: ﴿And We chose them knowingly over the worlds﴾, meaning: Allah chose them over the worlds of their time, with knowledge of their worthiness for that. The intended meaning is not that He chose them over all the worlds, by the evidence of His saying concerning this nation: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 110]. It was also said: over all the worlds, because of the multitude of prophets among them. The position of "ʿalā ʿilm" is accusative as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "ikhtarnāhum," i.e., "our choosing them was with knowledge from Us," and "ʿalā al-ʿālamīn" is connected to "ikhtarnāhum."

﴿And We gave them of the signs﴾, meaning: the miracles of Musa, ﴿in which there was a manifest trial﴾, meaning: a clear test and an evident examination, to see how they would act.

Qatadah said: the signs were their deliverance from drowning, the splitting of the sea for them, the shading of the cloud over them, and the sending down of manna and quail upon them.

Ibn Zayd said: the signs are the evil from which He restrained them and the good He commanded them to do.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "the manifest trial" is the clear favour, as in His saying: ﴿and that He might bestow upon the believers from Him a good favour﴾, and from it is Zuhayr's saying:

*So He gave them both the best of favours, which tries.*

The reference in His saying "indeed these" is to the disbelievers of Quraysh, because the discourse concerns them, and the story of Pharaoh is brought to show that they are equal in persistence in disbelief.

﴿Indeed they say: "It is only our first death"﴾ (p-1353), meaning: it is only our first death, which we die in this world, and there is no life after it, nor resurrection. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and we shall not be resurrected﴾, meaning: raised again. There is no intention in the speech to affirm another death; rather the meaning is: the outcome and end of the matter is only the first death, which removes worldly life. Al-Razi said: the meaning is that there will not come upon us from severe conditions except the first death.

Then they put forward against the one who promised them resurrection what they took to be evidence, but it is a defeated argument, and they said: ﴿Then bring our fathers﴾, meaning: return them after their death to the world, ﴿if you are truthful﴾ in what you say and tell us about resurrection.

Then Allah, glorified is He, answered them with His saying: ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba'?﴾, meaning: are they better in strength and power, or the people of Tubba' the Himyarite, who ruled the world with his armies, overcame its people and subdued them? In this is a severe threat. It was said: the intended meaning of "the people of Tubba'" is all his followers, not one specific person.

Al-Farra' said: The address in His words, ﴿So bring back our fathers﴾, is to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ alone, like His words, ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99]. The more preferable view is that it is addressed to him and to his followers among the Muslims. "And" the intended meaning of ﴿those before them﴾ is ʿĀd, Thamūd and their likes. His words, "We destroyed them," form a new independent clause explaining their state and the outcome of their affair. The clause ﴿Indeed, they were criminals﴾ gives the reason for their destruction. The meaning is: Allah, glorified is He, destroyed these people because they were criminals; so His destroying one who is lower than them, because he is a criminal, while being weaker and having less power, is all the more fitting.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words, ﴿And We had certainly tested﴾, that he said: "We tested before them the people of Pharaoh, and there came to them a noble Messenger," he said: "He is Moses." ﴿Deliver to me the servants of Allah﴾: send with me the Children of Israel. ﴿And do not exalt yourselves against Allah﴾: he said, "Do not transgress." ﴿Indeed, I bring you a clear authority﴾: he said, "a clear excuse." ﴿And indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord, lest you stone me﴾: he said, "with stones." ﴿And if you do not believe me, then leave me alone﴾: that is, leave my way.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, regarding His words, ﴿Deliver to me the servants of Allah﴾, that he said: "It means: follow me to the truth to which I invite you." Regarding His words, ﴿And do not exalt yourselves against Allah﴾, he said: "Do not fabricate lies." And regarding His words, ﴿lest you stone me﴾, he said: "lest you revile me."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also, regarding His words, ﴿rahwan﴾, he said: "a course (samt)."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also, regarding ﴿rahwan﴾, he said: "as it is in its state; and pass through it."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also, that he asked Ka'b about His words, ﴿And leave the sea rahwan﴾, and he said: "a path."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas, also, that he said: "Rahw is that it is left as it was."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also, regarding His words, ﴿and a noble station﴾, that he said: "the pulpits." Ibn Mardawayh related the like of it from Jabir.

al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and al-Khatib related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no servant but that he has two doors: a door through which his deed ascends, and a door through which his provision descends. When he dies, they both miss him and weep over him." And he recited this verse: ﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep over them﴾. He mentioned that they had not done any righteous deed on the earth for which it would weep over them, and no good word of theirs or of their deeds had ascended to the heaven, so that it would miss them and weep over them.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related something similar from the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas.

Abu al-Shaykh related from him, who said: It is said: "The earth weeps over the believer for forty mornings."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Jarir related from Shurayh ibn ʿUbayd al-Hadrami, as a mursal report, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, Islam began as a stranger and will return as a stranger, as it began. Certainly, there is no strangeness upon a believer. No believer dies in a strangeness in which his weepers are absent from him there, except that the heaven and the earth weep over him." Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: ﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep over them﴾. Then he said: "Indeed, they do not weep over a disbeliever."

Ibn al-Mubarak, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi al-Dunya, through the route of al-Musayyab ibn Rafi', related from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, who said: "Indeed, when the believer dies, his place of prayer on the earth weeps over him, and the ascent of his deed from the heaven." Then he recited the verse.

Ibn al-Mubarak, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Indeed, the earth weeps over the son of Adam for forty mornings." Then he recited the verse.

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Do not revile Tubba', for he has embraced Islam."

Ahmad, al-Tabarani, Ibn Majah and Ibn Mardawayh related it from Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, and he mentioned something similar. Something similar to this has been reported from others among the Companions and the Successors.

And We had certainly tested before them the people of Pharaoh, meaning: We tried them. The sense of "fitnah" (testing) here is that Allah, glorified is He, sent to them His messengers, and they commanded them with what He had prescribed for them, but they denied them; or He expanded their provisions, so they transgressed and oppressed.

Al-Zajjaj said: "We tested them." The meaning: We dealt with them as one deals with someone being tried, by sending the messengers to them. It is also read "fattannā" with the doubled letter. ﴿And there came to them a noble messenger﴾, meaning: noble with Allah and noble among his people. Muqatil said: good of character, through forgiveness and pardon. Al-Farra' said: noble with his Lord, since He singled him out with prophethood.

﴿Deliver to me the servants of Allah﴾. "An" here is the explanatory "an" (al-mufassirah, "that/namely"), because what precedes has the sense of speech. It may also be the light form (al-mukhaffafah) of the heavy "inna", meaning: "Indeed, the matter and the word is: deliver to me the servants of Allah." It may also be the verbal "an" (maṣdariyyah), meaning: "by [the command] 'deliver'," the sense being that he asked them to hand over to him the Children of Israel. Mujahid said: the meaning is "Send with me the servants of Allah and release them from the punishment," so "the servants of Allah" in this case is the direct object.

It was also said: the meaning is "Deliver to me the servants of Allah what is due upon you of the rights of Allah," in which case it is in the accusative as an annexed vocative.

It was also said: "Deliver to me your hearing until I convey to you the message of your Lord." ﴿Indeed I am to you a trustworthy messenger﴾: this is a reason for what precedes, i.e., a messenger from Allah to you, trustworthy regarding the message, not to be accused.

﴿And do not exalt yourselves against Allah﴾, meaning: do not be arrogant and haughty toward Him by raising yourselves above obeying Him and following His messengers. It was said: do not transgress against Allah; it was said: do not fabricate against Him. The first is preferable, and Ibn Juraij and Yahya ibn Salam said so. The clause ﴿Indeed I bring you a clear authority﴾ is a reason for the prohibition before it, i.e., with a clear proof that there is no way to deny. Qatadah said: with a clear excuse. The first is preferable, and Yahya ibn Salam said so.

The majority read "inni" with a kasra on the hamza; it is also read with a fatha, by supposing the lam (li-anna).

﴿And indeed I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord, lest you stone me﴾. He sought refuge in Allah, glorified is He, when they threatened him with killing; the meaning is "from your stoning me."

Qatadah said: "You stone me with stones." It was said: "You revile me." It was said: "You kill me."

﴿And if you do not believe me, then leave me alone﴾, meaning: if you do not affirm me and acknowledge my prophethood, then leave me and do not molest me.

Muqatil said: "Leave me as a neutral matter, neither against me nor for me." It was said: "Be apart from me, and I am apart from you until Allah judges between us." It was said: "Then let my way be." The meanings are close.

Then, when they did not affirm him and did not answer his call, he returned to his Lord with supplication, as Allah related of him in His saying: ﴿So he called upon his Lord, that these are a criminal people.﴾ The majority read the hamza with a fatha, by supposing a dropped preposition, i.e., "he called upon Him with [the statement] that these are..." The "mujrimun" are the disbelievers. He called it supplication even though he mentioned only the fact of their being criminals, because they had by that deserved his supplication against them.

It was also said: over all the worlds, because of the multitude of prophets among them. ﴿And We gave them of the signs﴾, meaning: the miracles of Musa, ﴿in which there was a manifest trial﴾, meaning: a clear test and an evident examination, to see how they would act.

Qatadah said: the signs were their deliverance from drowning, the splitting of the sea for them, the shading of the cloud over them, and the sending down of manna and quail upon them.

Ibn Zayd said: the signs are the evil from which He restrained them and the good He commanded them to do.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "the manifest trial" is the clear favour, as in His saying: ﴿and that He might bestow upon the believers from Him a good favour﴾, and from it is Zuhayr's saying:

*So He gave them both the best of favours, which tries.*

The reference in His saying "indeed these" is to the disbelievers of Quraysh, because the discourse concerns them, and the story of Pharaoh is brought to show that they are equal in persistence in disbelief.

﴿Indeed they say: "It is only our first death"﴾ (p-1353), meaning: it is only our first death, which we die in this world, and there is no life after it, nor resurrection. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and we shall not be resurrected﴾, meaning: raised again. There is no intention in the speech to affirm another death; rather the meaning is: the outcome and end of the matter is only the first death, which removes worldly life. Al-Razi said: the meaning is that there will not come upon us from severe conditions except the first death.

Then they put forward against the one who promised them resurrection what they took to be evidence, but it is a defeated argument, and they said: ﴿Then bring our fathers﴾, meaning: return them after their death to the world, ﴿if you are truthful﴾ in what you say and tell us about resurrection.

Then Allah, glorified is He, answered them with His saying: ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba'?﴾, meaning: are they better in strength and power, or the people of Tubba' the Himyarite, who ruled the world with his armies, overcame its people and subdued them? In this is a severe threat. It was said: the intended meaning of "the people of Tubba'" is all his followers, not one specific person.

Al-Farra' said: The address in His words, ﴿So bring back our fathers﴾, is to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ alone, like His words, ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99]. The more preferable view is that it is addressed to him and to his followers among the Muslims. "And" the intended meaning of ﴿those before them﴾ is ʿĀd, Thamūd and their likes. His words, "We destroyed them," form a new independent clause explaining their state and the outcome of their affair. The clause ﴿Indeed, they were criminals﴾ gives the reason for their destruction. The meaning is: Allah, glorified is He, destroyed these people because they were criminals; so His destroying one who is lower than them, because he is a criminal, while being weaker and having less power, is all the more fitting.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words, ﴿And We had certainly tested﴾, that he said: "We tested before them the people of Pharaoh, and there came to them a noble Messenger," he said: "He is Moses." ﴿Deliver to me the servants of Allah﴾: send with me the Children of Israel. ﴿And do not exalt yourselves against Allah﴾: he said, "Do not transgress." ﴿Indeed, I bring you a clear authority﴾: he said, "a clear excuse." ﴿And indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord, lest you stone me﴾: he said, "with stones." ﴿And if you do not believe me, then leave me alone﴾: that is, leave my way.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, regarding His words, ﴿Deliver to me the servants of Allah﴾, that he said: "It means: follow me to the truth to which I invite you." Regarding His words, ﴿And do not exalt yourselves against Allah﴾, he said: "Do not fabricate lies." And regarding His words, ﴿lest you stone me﴾, he said: "lest you revile me."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also, regarding His words, ﴿rahwan﴾, he said: "a course (samt)."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also, regarding ﴿rahwan﴾, he said: "as it is in its state; and pass through it."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also, that he asked Ka'b about His words, ﴿And leave the sea rahwan﴾, and he said: "a path."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas, also, that he said: "Rahw is that it is left as it was."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also, regarding His words, ﴿and a noble station﴾, that he said: "the pulpits." Ibn Mardawayh related the like of it from Jabir.

al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and al-Khatib related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no servant but that he has two doors: a door through which his deed ascends, and a door through which his provision descends. When he dies, they both miss him and weep over him." And he recited this verse: ﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep over them﴾. He mentioned that they had not done any righteous deed on the earth for which it would weep over them, and no good word of theirs or of their deeds had ascended to the heaven, so that it would miss them and weep over them.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related something similar from the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas.

Abu al-Shaykh related from him, who said: It is said: "The earth weeps over the believer for forty mornings."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Jarir related from Shurayh ibn ʿUbayd al-Hadrami, as a mursal report, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, Islam began as a stranger and will return as a stranger, as it began. Certainly, there is no strangeness upon a believer. No believer dies in a strangeness in which his weepers are absent from him there, except that the heaven and the earth weep over him." Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: ﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep over them﴾. Then he said: "Indeed, they do not weep over a disbeliever."

Ibn al-Mubarak, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi al-Dunya, through the route of al-Musayyab ibn Rafi', related from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, who said: "Indeed, when the believer dies, his place of prayer on the earth weeps over him, and the ascent of his deed from the heaven." Then he recited the verse.

Ibn al-Mubarak, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Indeed, the earth weeps over the son of Adam for forty mornings." Then he recited the verse.

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Do not revile Tubba', for he has embraced Islam."

Ahmad, al-Tabarani, Ibn Majah and Ibn Mardawayh related it from Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, and he mentioned something similar. Something similar to this has been reported from others among the Companions and the Successors.

And We had certainly tested before them the people of Pharaoh, meaning: We tried them. The sense of "fitnah" (testing) here is that Allah, glorified is He, sent to them His messengers, and they commanded them with what He had prescribed for them, but they denied them; or He expanded their provisions, so they transgressed and oppressed.

Al-Zajjaj said: "We tested them." The meaning: We dealt with them as one deals with someone being tried, by sending the messengers to them. It is also read "fattannā" with the doubled letter. ﴿And there came to them a noble messenger﴾, meaning: noble with Allah and noble among his people. Muqatil said: good of character, through forgiveness and pardon. Al-Farra' said: noble with his Lord, since He singled him out with prophethood.

﴿Deliver to me the servants of Allah﴾. "An" here is the explanatory "an" (al-mufassirah, "that/namely"), because what precedes has the sense of speech. It may also be the light form (al-mukhaffafah) of the heavy "inna", meaning: "Indeed, the matter and the word is: deliver to me the servants of Allah." It may also be the verbal "an" (maṣdariyyah), meaning: "by [the command] 'deliver'," the sense being that he asked them to hand over to him the Children of Israel. Mujahid said: the meaning is "Send with me the servants of Allah and release them from the punishment," so "the servants of Allah" in this case is the direct object.

It was also said: the meaning is "Deliver to me the servants of Allah what is due upon you of the rights of Allah," in which case it is in the accusative as an annexed vocative.

It was also said: "Deliver to me your hearing until I convey to you the message of your Lord." ﴿Indeed I am to you a trustworthy messenger﴾: this is a reason for what precedes, i.e., a messenger from Allah to you, trustworthy regarding the message, not to be accused.

﴿And do not exalt yourselves against Allah﴾, meaning: do not be arrogant and haughty toward Him by raising yourselves above obeying Him and following His messengers. It was said: do not transgress against Allah; it was said: do not fabricate against Him. The first is preferable, and Ibn Juraij and Yahya ibn Salam said so. The clause ﴿Indeed I bring you a clear authority﴾ is a reason for the prohibition before it, i.e., with a clear proof that there is no way to deny. Qatadah said: with a clear excuse. The first is preferable, and Yahya ibn Salam said so.

The majority read "inni" with a kasra on the hamza; it is also read with a fatha, by supposing the lam (li-anna).

﴿And indeed I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord, lest you stone me﴾. He sought refuge in Allah, glorified is He, when they threatened him with killing; the meaning is "from your stoning me."

Qatadah said: "You stone me with stones." It was said: "You revile me." It was said: "You kill me."

﴿And if you do not believe me, then leave me alone﴾, meaning: if you do not affirm me and acknowledge my prophethood, then leave me and do not molest me.

Muqatil said: "Leave me as a neutral matter, neither against me nor for me." It was said: "Be apart from me, and I am apart from you until Allah judges between us." It was said: "Then let my way be." The meanings are close.

Then, when they did not affirm him and did not answer his call, he returned to his Lord with supplication, as Allah related of him in His saying: ﴿So he called upon his Lord, that these are a criminal people.﴾ The majority read the hamza with a fatha, by supposing a dropped preposition, i.e., "he called upon Him with [the statement] that these are..." Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Isa ibn Umar read it with a kasra, by supposing "saying." In the speech there is an ellipsis, i.e., "so they disbelieved, so he called upon his Lord." The "mujrimun" are the disbelievers. He called it supplication even though he mentioned only the fact of their being criminals, because they had by that deserved his supplication against them.

﴿So travel by night with My servants﴾. Allah, glorified is He, answered his supplication, and commanded that he travel by night with the Children of Israel. It is said "sara" and "asra," both being dialectal forms. The majority read "fa-asri" with a cut (hamzat al-qat'), and the people of the Hijaz read it with a wasl (linking), and Ibn Kathir agreed with them. So the first reading is from "asra," and the second from "sara." The clause is by supposing "saying," i.e., Allah said to Musa: "Travel by night with My servants." ﴿Indeed you will be pursued﴾, meaning: Pharaoh and his hosts will follow you, and the departure of Pharaoh after them has been mentioned in more than one place.

﴿And leave the sea parted﴾, meaning: still, as is said: "raha yarhu rahwan" when it becomes still and does not move.

Al-Jawhari said: it is said "af'al dhalika rahwan," meaning: calmly, in your state; and "ʿaysh rāh," meaning: still. "Raha al-bahr" means the sea became still. Al-Harawi and others said likewise, and this is the known meaning in the language. From it is the poet's saying:

*And the horses prance rahwan in their bridles, like birds escaping from the shurnub with its fur.*

That is: the horses prance in their bridles while still. The meaning is: leave the sea still in its state after you have struck it with your staff, and do not command it to return, as it was, so that the family of Pharaoh enter it after you and after the Children of Israel, (p-1352) and it close over them, and they drown.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "raha bayna rijlayhi rahwan," meaning: he opened them wide. He said: from it is His saying: ﴿And leave the sea parted﴾, meaning: leave it open, as it was after your entering into it. Abu 'Ubayd said likewise, and Mujahid and others said so. Ibn 'Arafa said: both return to one meaning, even if their wording differs, because when the sea's flow is still, it opens. Al-Harawi said: it is possible that "rahwan" is an adjective for Musa, i.e., "travel calmly in your state." Ka'b and al-Hasan said "rahwan" means "a path." Al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' said: "easy."

ʿIkrima said: "dry," as in His saying: ﴿So strike for them a dry path in the sea﴾ [Ta-Ha: 77]. On every reckoning, the meaning is: leave it in a state of rahw, or leave it "rahwan," for emphasis in describing by the verbal noun. ﴿Indeed they are a drowned host﴾, meaning: indeed Pharaoh and his people are drowned.

Allah, glorified is He, informed Musa of this so that his heart would be at rest and his resolve would be steadied.

The majority read "inna" with a kasra as a fresh sentence, for the purpose of informing of this; it is also read with a fatha, by supposing "li-annahum."

﴿How many they left behind of gardens and springs﴾: "kam" here is the informative "kam," which indicates multiplicity. The discussion of the meaning of this verse has passed in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

The majority read "wa-maqamin" with a fatha on the mim, as a noun of place for standing. Ibn Hurmuz, Qatadah, al-Sumayfa', and it is reported from Nafi' with a damma, meaning a place of dwelling.

﴿And luxury in which they were fruit-eaters/merry﴾. "Nima" with a fatha means luxury (al-tanaʿʿum): it is said "naʿʿamahu Allah" and "nāʿamahu," so he became luxurious. With a kasra it means favour (al-minnah) and what Allah bestowed upon you; "fulan wasi' al-ni'mah" means he is wealthy. Al-Jawhari mentioned this meaning.

The majority read "fakihin" with an alif. Abu Raja', al-Hasan, Abu al-Ashhab, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, and Shayba read "fakihin" without an alif. The meaning in the first reading is: enjoying luxury, their souls content; in the second: insolent and wanton.

Al-Jawhari said: "fakiha al-rajul" with a kasra means he is "fakih" when he is good-natured and joking; "al-fakih" also means insolent and wanton. He said: "wa-fakihin" means luxurious. Al-Tha'labi said: both are dialects, like "hadhir" and "hadhar," and "farih" and "farih." It was said: "al-fakih" is one who enjoys all kinds of pleasure, as a man enjoys all kinds of fruit.

﴿Thus, and We made them inherit another people﴾. The "ka" is in the nominative position, as a predicate of an omitted subject. Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., "the matter is thus." It may also be in the accusative position, with the reference being to the verbal noun of a verb indicated by "they left," i.e., "like that deprivation We deprived them of it." It was also said: "like that expulsion We expelled them from it," and it was said: "like that destruction We destroyed them."

On the first reading, "wa-awrathnaha" is coordinated with "taraku"; on the latter readings, it is coordinated with the supposed verb.

By "another people" is meant the Children of Israel, for Allah made them possess the land of Egypt after they had been enslaved in it, so they became its inheritors, i.e., it came to them as inheritance comes to an heir. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿And We made the people who were oppressed inherit the eastern and western parts of the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 137].

﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep over them﴾. This is a statement of their being unconcerned by their destruction.

The exegetes said: that is, they had not been doing righteous deeds on earth for which the earth would weep over them, and no good deed of theirs ascended to heaven for which it would be wept over. The meaning is that no one among the people of heaven or the people of earth was afflicted by their loss and destruction. The Arabs used to say, upon the death of a chief among them: "the heaven and the earth wept for him," meaning his calamity was widespread. From this is Jarir's saying:

*When the news of al-Zubayr came, the walls of Madina humbled themselves, and the lofty mountains.*

From it is also al-Nabigha's saying:

*Harith al-Jawlan wept for the loss of his lord, and Hawran, humbled and shrunken, wept with him.*

Al-Hasan said: there is an omitted annexed noun in the speech, i.e., "the people of heaven and earth, of angels and men, did not weep over them."

Mujahid said: indeed the heaven and the earth weep over the believer for forty mornings. It was said: he is wept for by the places of his prayer and the ascending paths of his deeds. ﴿And they were not given respite﴾, meaning: not granted a delay to another time; rather they were hastened into punishment because of the extremity of their disbelief and the severity of their obstinacy.

﴿And indeed We delivered the Children of Israel from the humiliating punishment﴾, meaning: We rescued them, by destroying their enemy, from what they were in of enslavement, the killing of sons, the sparing of women, and the imposition of hard labour upon them.

His saying "from Pharaoh" is an apposition to "the punishment," either by an omitted annexed noun, i.e., "from the punishment of Pharaoh," or for emphasis, as if he were the punishment itself, so it is substituted for it; or it is a circumstantial clause of "the punishment," the sense being "issuing from Pharaoh." Ibn 'Abbas read "man Fir'awn" with a fatha on the mim, as an interrogative of contempt, as one says to someone who boasts of his lineage or ancestry: "Who are you?"

Then He, glorified is He, explained his condition, saying: ﴿Indeed he was haughty among the extravagant﴾, meaning: haughty in arrogance and tyranny, among the extravagant in disbelief in Allah and in committing His sins, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4].

When He, glorified is He, explained the manner in which He removed harm from the Children of Israel, He explained what He honoured them with, saying: ﴿And We chose them knowingly over the worlds﴾, meaning: Allah chose them over the worlds of their time, with knowledge of their worthiness for that. The intended meaning is not that He chose them over all the worlds, by the evidence of His saying concerning this nation: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 110]. It was also said: over all the worlds, because of the multitude of prophets among them. The position of "ʿalā ʿilm" is accusative as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "ikhtarnāhum," i.e., "our choosing them was with knowledge from Us," and "ʿalā al-ʿālamīn" is connected to "ikhtarnāhum."

﴿And We gave them of the signs﴾, meaning: the miracles of Musa, ﴿in which there was a manifest trial﴾, meaning: a clear test and an evident examination, to see how they would act.

Qatadah said: the signs were their deliverance from drowning, the splitting of the sea for them, the shading of the cloud over them, and the sending down of manna and quail upon them.

*So He gave them both the best of favours, which tries.*

﴿Indeed they say: "It is only our first death"﴾ (p-1353), meaning: it is only our first death, which we die in this world, and there is no life after it, nor resurrection. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and we shall not be resurrected﴾, meaning: raised again. Mujahid said: the meaning is "Send with me the servants of Allah and release them from the punishment," so "the servants of Allah" in this case is the direct object.

It was also said: the meaning is "Deliver to me the servants of Allah what is due upon you of the rights of Allah," in which case it is in the accusative as an annexed vocative.

It was also said: "Deliver to me your hearing until I convey to you the message of your Lord." ﴿Indeed I am to you a trustworthy messenger﴾: this is a reason for what precedes, i.e., a messenger from Allah to you, trustworthy regarding the message, not to be accused.

﴿And do not exalt yourselves against Allah﴾, meaning: do not be arrogant and haughty toward Him by raising yourselves above obeying Him and following His messengers. It was said: do not transgress against Allah; it was said: do not fabricate against Him. The first is preferable, and Ibn Juraij and Yahya ibn Salam said so. The clause ﴿Indeed I bring you a clear authority﴾ is a reason for the prohibition before it, i.e., with a clear proof that there is no way to deny. Qatadah said: with a clear excuse. The first is preferable, and Yahya ibn Salam said so.

The majority read "inni" with a kasra on the hamza; it is also read with a fatha, by supposing the lam (li-anna).

﴿And indeed I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord, lest you stone me﴾. He sought refuge in Allah, glorified is He, when they threatened him with killing; the meaning is "from your stoning me."

Qatadah said: "You stone me with stones." It was said: "You revile me." It was said: "You kill me."

﴿And if you do not believe me, then leave me alone﴾, meaning: if you do not affirm me and acknowledge my prophethood, then leave me and do not molest me.

Muqatil said: "Leave me as a neutral matter, neither against me nor for me." It was said: "Be apart from me, and I am apart from you until Allah judges between us." It was said: "Then let my way be." The meanings are close.

Then, when they did not affirm him and did not answer his call, he returned to his Lord with supplication, as Allah related of him in His saying: ﴿So he called upon his Lord, that these are a criminal people.﴾ The majority read the hamza with a fatha, by supposing a dropped preposition, i.e., "he called upon Him with [the statement] that these are..." Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Isa ibn Umar read it with a kasra, by supposing "saying." In the speech there is an ellipsis, i.e., "so they disbelieved, so he called upon his Lord." The "mujrimun" are the disbelievers. He called it supplication even though he mentioned only the fact of their being criminals, because they had by that deserved his supplication against them.

﴿So travel by night with My servants﴾. Allah, glorified is He, answered his supplication, and commanded that he travel by night with the Children of Israel. It is said "sara" and "asra," both being dialectal forms. The majority read "fa-asri" with a cut (hamzat al-qat'), and the people of the Hijaz read it with a wasl (linking), and Ibn Kathir agreed with them. So the first reading is from "asra," and the second from "sara." The clause is by supposing "saying," i.e., Allah said to Musa: "Travel by night with My servants." ﴿Indeed you will be pursued﴾, meaning: Pharaoh and his hosts will follow you, and the departure of Pharaoh after them has been mentioned in more than one place.

﴿And leave the sea parted﴾, meaning: still, as is said: "raha yarhu rahwan" when it becomes still and does not move.

Al-Jawhari said: it is said "af'al dhalika rahwan," meaning: calmly, in your state; and "ʿaysh rāh," meaning: still. "Raha al-bahr" means the sea became still. Al-Harawi and others said likewise, and this is the known meaning in the language. From it is the poet's saying:

*And the horses prance rahwan in their bridles, like birds escaping from the shurnub with its fur.*

That is: the horses prance in their bridles while still. The meaning is: leave the sea still in its state after you have struck it with your staff, and do not command it to return, as it was, so that the family of Pharaoh enter it after you and after the Children of Israel, (p-1352) and it close over them, and they drown.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "raha bayna rijlayhi rahwan," meaning: he opened them wide. He said: from it is His saying: ﴿And leave the sea parted﴾, meaning: leave it open, as it was after your entering into it. Abu 'Ubayd said likewise, and Mujahid and others said so. Ibn 'Arafa said: both return to one meaning, even if their wording differs, because when the sea's flow is still, it opens. Al-Harawi said: it is possible that "rahwan" is an adjective for Musa, i.e., "travel calmly in your state." Ka'b and al-Hasan said "rahwan" means "a path." Al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' said: "easy."

ʿIkrima said: "dry," as in His saying: ﴿So strike for them a dry path in the sea﴾ [Ta-Ha: 77]. On every reckoning, the meaning is: leave it in a state of rahw, or leave it "rahwan," for emphasis in describing by the verbal noun. ﴿Indeed they are a drowned host﴾, meaning: indeed Pharaoh and his people are drowned.

Allah, glorified is He, informed Musa of this so that his heart would be at rest and his resolve would be steadied.

The majority read "inna" with a kasra as a fresh sentence, for the purpose of informing of this; it is also read with a fatha, by supposing "li-annahum."

﴿How many they left behind of gardens and springs﴾: "kam" here is the informative "kam," which indicates multiplicity. The discussion of the meaning of this verse has passed in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

The majority read "wa-maqamin" with a fatha on the mim, as a noun of place for standing. Ibn Hurmuz, Qatadah, al-Sumayfa', and it is reported from Nafi' with a damma, meaning a place of dwelling.

﴿And luxury in which they were fruit-eaters/merry﴾. "Nima" with a fatha means luxury (al-tanaʿʿum): it is said "naʿʿamahu Allah" and "nāʿamahu," so he became luxurious. With a kasra it means favour (al-minnah) and what Allah bestowed upon you; "fulan wasi' al-ni'mah" means he is wealthy. Al-Jawhari mentioned this meaning.

The majority read "fakihin" with an alif. Abu Raja', al-Hasan, Abu al-Ashhab, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, and Shayba read "fakihin" without an alif. The meaning in the first reading is: enjoying luxury, their souls content; in the second: insolent and wanton.

Al-Jawhari said: "fakiha al-rajul" with a kasra means he is "fakih" when he is good-natured and joking; "al-fakih" also means insolent and wanton. He said: "wa-fakihin" means luxurious. Al-Tha'labi said: both are dialects, like "hadhir" and "hadhar," and "farih" and "farih." It was said: "al-fakih" is one who enjoys all kinds of pleasure, as a man enjoys all kinds of fruit.

﴿Thus, and We made them inherit another people﴾. The "ka" is in the nominative position, as a predicate of an omitted subject. Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., "the matter is thus." It may also be in the accusative position, with the reference being to the verbal noun of a verb indicated by "they left," i.e., "like that deprivation We deprived them of it." It was also said: "like that expulsion We expelled them from it," and it was said: "like that destruction We destroyed them."

On the first reading, "wa-awrathnaha" is coordinated with "taraku"; on the latter readings, it is coordinated with the supposed verb.

By "another people" is meant the Children of Israel, for Allah made them possess the land of Egypt after they had been enslaved in it, so they became its inheritors, i.e., it came to them as inheritance comes to an heir. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿And We made the people who were oppressed inherit the eastern and western parts of the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 137].

﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep over them﴾. This is a statement of their being unconcerned by their destruction.

The exegetes said: that is, they had not been doing righteous deeds on earth for which the earth would weep over them, and no good deed of theirs ascended to heaven for which it would be wept over. The meaning is that no one among the people of heaven or the people of earth was afflicted by their loss and destruction. The Arabs used to say, upon the death of a chief among them: "the heaven and the earth wept for him," meaning his calamity was widespread. From this is Jarir's saying:

*When the news of al-Zubayr came, the walls of Madina humbled themselves, and the lofty mountains.*

From it is also al-Nabigha's saying:

*Harith al-Jawlan wept for the loss of his lord, and Hawran, humbled and shrunken, wept with him.*

Al-Hasan said: there is an omitted annexed noun in the speech, i.e., "the people of heaven and earth, of angels and men, did not weep over them."

Mujahid said: indeed the heaven and the earth weep over the believer for forty mornings. It was said: he is wept for by the places of his prayer and the ascending paths of his deeds. ﴿And they were not given respite﴾, meaning: not granted a delay to another time; rather they were hastened into punishment because of the extremity of their disbelief and the severity of their obstinacy.

﴿And indeed We delivered the Children of Israel from the humiliating punishment﴾, meaning: We rescued them, by destroying their enemy, from what they were in of enslavement, the killing of sons, the sparing of women, and the imposition of hard labour upon them.

His saying "from Pharaoh" is an apposition to "the punishment," either by an omitted annexed noun, i.e., "from the punishment of Pharaoh," or for emphasis, as if he were the punishment itself, so it is substituted for it; or it is a circumstantial clause of "the punishment," the sense being "issuing from Pharaoh." Ibn 'Abbas read "man Fir'awn" with a fatha on the mim, as an interrogative of contempt, as one says to someone who boasts of his lineage or ancestry: "Who are you?"

Then He, glorified is He, explained his condition, saying: ﴿Indeed he was haughty among the extravagant﴾, meaning: haughty in arrogance and tyranny, among the extravagant in disbelief in Allah and in committing His sins, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 4].

When He, glorified is He, explained the manner in which He removed harm from the Children of Israel, He explained what He honoured them with, saying: ﴿And We chose them knowingly over the worlds﴾, meaning: Allah chose them over the worlds of their time, with knowledge of their worthiness for that. The intended meaning is not that He chose them over all the worlds, by the evidence of His saying concerning this nation: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 110]. It was also said: over all the worlds, because of the multitude of prophets among them. The position of "ʿalā ʿilm" is accusative as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "ikhtarnāhum," i.e., "our choosing them was with knowledge from Us," and "ʿalā al-ʿālamīn" is connected to "ikhtarnāhum."

﴿And We gave them of the signs﴾, meaning: the miracles of Musa, ﴿in which there was a manifest trial﴾, meaning: a clear test and an evident examination, to see how they would act.

Qatadah said: the signs were their deliverance from drowning, the splitting of the sea for them, the shading of the cloud over them, and the sending down of manna and quail upon them.

Ibn Zayd said: the signs are the evil from which He restrained them and the good He commanded them to do.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "the manifest trial" is the clear favour, as in His saying: ﴿and that He might bestow upon the believers from Him a good favour﴾, and from it is Zuhayr's saying:

*So He gave them both the best of favours, which tries.*

The reference in His saying "indeed these" is to the disbelievers of Quraysh, because the discourse concerns them, and the story of Pharaoh is brought to show that they are equal in persistence in disbelief.

﴿Indeed they say: "It is only our first death"﴾ (p-1353), meaning: it is only our first death, which we die in this world, and there is no life after it, nor resurrection. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and we shall not be resurrected﴾, meaning: raised again. There is no intention in the speech to affirm another death; rather the meaning is: the outcome and end of the matter is only the first death, which removes worldly life. Al-Razi said: the meaning is that there will not come upon us from severe conditions except the first death.

Then they put forward against the one who promised them resurrection what they took to be evidence, but it is a defeated argument, and they said: ﴿Then bring our fathers﴾, meaning: return them after their death to the world, ﴿if you are truthful﴾ in what you say and tell us about resurrection.

Then Allah, glorified is He, answered them with His saying: ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba'?﴾, meaning: are they better in strength and power, or the people of Tubba' the Himyarite, who ruled the world with his armies, overcame its people and subdued them? In this is a severe threat. It was said: the intended meaning of "the people of Tubba'" is all his followers, not one specific person.

Al-Farra' said: The address in His words, ﴿So bring back our fathers﴾, is to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ alone, like His words, ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99]. The more preferable view is that it is addressed to him and to his followers among the Muslims. "And" the intended meaning of ﴿those before them﴾ is ʿĀd, Thamūd and their likes. His words, "We destroyed them," form a new independent clause explaining their state and the outcome of their affair. The clause ﴿Indeed, they were criminals﴾ gives the reason for their destruction. The meaning is: Allah, glorified is He, destroyed these people because they were criminals; so His destroying one who is lower than them, because he is a criminal, while being weaker and having less power, is all the more fitting.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words, ﴿And We had certainly tested﴾, that he said: "We tested before them the people of Pharaoh, and there came to them a noble Messenger," he said: "He is Moses." ﴿Deliver to me the servants of Allah﴾: send with me the Children of Israel. ﴿And do not exalt yourselves against Allah﴾: he said, "Do not transgress." ﴿Indeed, I bring you a clear authority﴾: he said, "a clear excuse." ﴿And indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord, lest you stone me﴾: he said, "with stones." ﴿And if you do not believe me, then leave me alone﴾: that is, leave my way.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, regarding His words, ﴿Deliver to me the servants of Allah﴾, that he said: "It means: follow me to the truth to which I invite you." Regarding His words, ﴿And do not exalt yourselves against Allah﴾, he said: "Do not fabricate lies." And regarding His words, ﴿lest you stone me﴾, he said: "lest you revile me."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also, regarding His words, ﴿rahwan﴾, he said: "a course (samt)."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also, regarding ﴿rahwan﴾, he said: "as it is in its state; and pass through it."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also, that he asked Ka'b about His words, ﴿And leave the sea rahwan﴾, and he said: "a path."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas, also, that he said: "Rahw is that it is left as it was."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, also, regarding His words, ﴿and a noble station﴾, that he said: "the pulpits." Ibn Mardawayh related the like of it from Jabir.

al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and al-Khatib related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no servant but that he has two doors: a door through which his deed ascends, and a door through which his provision descends. When he dies, they both miss him and weep over him." And he recited this verse: ﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep over them﴾. He mentioned that they had not done any righteous deed on the earth for which it would weep over them, and no good word of theirs or of their deeds had ascended to the heaven, so that it would miss them and weep over them.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related something similar from the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas.

Abu al-Shaykh related from him, who said: It is said: "The earth weeps over the believer for forty mornings."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Jarir related from Shurayh ibn ʿUbayd al-Hadrami, as a mursal report, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, Islam began as a stranger and will return as a stranger, as it began. Certainly, there is no strangeness upon a believer. No believer dies in a strangeness in which his weepers are absent from him there, except that the heaven and the earth weep over him." Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: ﴿So the heaven and the earth did not weep over them﴾. Then he said: "Indeed, they do not weep over a disbeliever."

Ibn al-Mubarak, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi al-Dunya, through the route of al-Musayyab ibn Rafi', related from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, who said: "Indeed, when the believer dies, his place of prayer on the earth weeps over him, and the ascent of his deed from the heaven." Then he recited the verse.

Ibn al-Mubarak, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Indeed, the earth weeps over the son of Adam for forty mornings." Then he recited the verse.

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Do not revile Tubba', for he has embraced Islam."

Ahmad, al-Tabarani, Ibn Majah and Ibn Mardawayh related it from Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, and he mentioned something similar. Something similar to this has been reported from others among the Companions and the Successors.

And We had certainly tested before them the people of Pharaoh, meaning: We tried them. The sense of "fitnah" (testing) here is that Allah, glorified is He, sent to them His messengers, and they commanded them with what He had prescribed for them, but they denied them; or He expanded their provisions, so they transgressed and oppressed.

Al-Zajjaj said: "We tested them." The meaning: We dealt with them as one deals with someone being tried, by sending the messengers to them. It is also read "fattannā" with the doubled letter. ﴿And there came to them a noble messenger﴾, meaning: noble with Allah and noble among his people. Muqatil said: good of character, through forgiveness and pardon. Al-Farra' said: noble with his Lord, since He singled him out with prophethood.

﴿Deliver to me the servants of Allah﴾. "An" here is the explanatory "an" (al-mufassirah, "that/namely"), because what precedes has the sense of speech. It may also be the light form (al-mukhaffafah) of the heavy "inna", meaning: "Indeed, the matter and the word is: deliver to me the servants of Allah." It may also be the verbal "an" (maṣdariyyah), meaning: "by [the command] 'deliver'," the sense being that he asked them to hand over to him the Children of Israel. Mujahid said: the meaning is "Send with me the servants of Allah and release them from the punishment," so "the servants of Allah" in this case is the direct object.

It was also said: the meaning is "Deliver to me the servants of Allah what is due upon you of the rights of Allah," in which case it is in the accusative as an annexed vocative.

It was also said: "Deliver to me your hearing until I convey to you the message of your Lord." ﴿Indeed I am to you a trustworthy messenger﴾: this is a reason for what precedes, i.e., a messenger from Allah to you, trustworthy regarding the message, not to be accused.

Qatadah said: "You stone me with stones." It was said: "You revile me." It was said: "You kill me."

﴿And if you do not believe me, then leave me alone﴾, meaning: if you do not affirm me and acknowledge my prophethood, then leave me and do not molest me.

Muqatil said: "Leave me as a neutral matter, neither against me nor for me." It was said: "Be apart from me, and I am apart from you until Allah judges between us." It was said: "Then let my way be." The meanings are close.

Then, when they did not affirm him and did not answer his call, he returned to his Lord with supplication, as Allah related of him in His saying: ﴿So he called upon his Lord, that these are a criminal people.﴾ The majority read the hamza with a fatha, by supposing a dropped preposition, i.e., "he called upon Him with [the statement] that these are..." The "mujrimun" are the disbelievers. He called it supplication even though he mentioned only the fact of their being criminals, because they had by that deserved his supplication against them.

﴿Thus, and We made them inherit another people﴾. The "ka" is in the nominative position, as a predicate of an omitted subject. Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., "the matter is thus."
